screens.body:
Concurrency means multiple things making progress at once — threads interleaving on one CPU, or truly in parallel on many cores.

It's how servers handle thousands of users and how your UI stays responsive during heavy work. Power — with sharp edges.

options: Lets multiple things make progress at once
Means one thing at a time
check.question: Concurrency…

screens.heading: What is concurrency?
screens.keyPoint: Many things progressing at once — powerful but sharp.

screens.body:
A race condition is when the result depends on which thread gets there first. Two threads read a balance of $100, both subtract $60, both write back $40. The real answer should be -$20 (overdraft!) — but the lost update hides it.

Races are the nastiest bugs: they happen rarely, can't be reproduced reliably, and corrupt data silently.

options: Makes the result depend on thread timing
check.question: A race condition…

screens.heading: Race conditions
screens.keyPoint: When timing decides the result, data gets corrupted.

screens.body:
The critical section is the code that touches shared data — the danger zone. The rule: only one thread inside at a time.

Everything else can run freely in parallel. You protect just the small shared-data part, keeping the rest fast.

options: Code touching shared data — one thread at a time
check.question: The critical section is…

screens.heading: The critical section
screens.keyPoint: Protect the small shared-data part; parallelize the rest.

screens.body:
A lock (mutex = mutual exclusion) guards the critical section. A thread locks it before entering and unlocks after leaving. Anyone else must wait their turn.

Think of a single-occupancy bathroom: lock the door, do your business, unlock. No lock, no privacy — and no correctness.

options: Lets only one thread into the critical section at a time
check.question: A mutex…

screens.heading: Locks (mutexes)
screens.keyPoint: Lock before, unlock after — one at a time.

screens.body:
A deadlock is when everyone waits forever. Thread A holds lock 1 and wants lock 2. Thread B holds lock 2 and wants lock 1. Neither will ever let go.

Deadlocks freeze programs silently — no crash, no error, just... nothing. The four ingredients: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait.

options: Threads waiting on each other forever
check.question: A deadlock is…

screens.heading: Deadlocks

screens.body:
The simplest prevention: always acquire locks in the same order, everywhere. If everyone takes lock 1 before lock 2, circular wait becomes impossible.

Other tools: timeouts (give up if a lock takes too long), and lock-free designs for experts. But consistent ordering solves most real cases.

check.question: Taking locks in the same order everywhere…

screens.heading: Avoiding deadlocks
screens.keyPoint: Consistent lock order kills circular wait.

screens.body:
SwiftGigs bidding: two taskers tap "accept" on the same task at the same instant. Without protection, both get assigned — a race condition with a real human consequence.

The fix is the same idea as a mutex: make "assign task" atomic — one winner, decided cleanly. Your database can enforce it with a transaction.

screens.keyPoint: Your bidding flow needs the same protection as a mutex.
